content: Running the server locally for development. The project builds as a single Maven module and needs Java 17 or newer on the path. From the mcp-server directory run mvn spring-boot:run and the application starts in the foreground with the web UI served from the same process on port 8080. Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 in a browser once the log prints that the application has started. There is no separate frontend server, no Node toolchain, and no npm install step: the browser-native HTML, CSS and JavaScript are served directly out of the classpath, so editing a file under static and reloading the page is enough to see the change. Hot restart is not configured; a change to Java code requires stopping the process with Ctrl-C and starting it again. The embedded SQLite database lives at data/mcpserver.db relative to the working directory and is created on first boot, so a fresh checkout needs no database setup. Deleting that file resets the workspace entirely, including uploaded files and ingested chunks. Development mode and production mode run exactly the same code path; the only difference is whether you launch through Maven or through the packaged archive.

Running the packaged application. Build the distributable with mvn package from the mcp-server directory, which produces target/mcp-server.jar containing the backend, the web UI and every dependency. Start it with java -jar target/mcp-server.jar. Java 17 or newer is required at runtime, the same minimum the build enforces. The server listens on port 8080 by default and binds to the loopback address 127.0.0.1. To listen on a different port pass --server.port=9090 as a program argument, or set the SERVER_PORT environment variable before launching; the argument form wins when both are present. The same override mechanism works for any configuration key in application.yml, so a deployment can retune retrieval or connector settings without rebuilding the archive. The working directory matters: the SQLite database, the downloaded plugin binaries and the credential key file are all resolved relative to it, so launch the archive from a stable directory rather than from a temporary one. Because everything ships inside one file there is no container image, no orchestration manifest and no external service to provision.

Running the server on Windows. The packaged archive behaves identically to macOS and Linux: install a Java 17 or newer runtime, open a terminal in the directory containing target\mcp-server.jar and run java -jar target\mcp-server.jar. The server listens on port 8080 bound to 127.0.0.1 and the web UI opens at the same address. Two things differ from Unix hosts. First, outbound HTTPS to internal systems uses the Windows Trusted Root Certification Authorities store in addition to the runtime's bundled certificate authorities, so an internal certificate already trusted by the operating system is trusted by the server without extra configuration. Second, paths in configuration must use backslashes or forward slashes consistently, and a path containing spaces has to be quoted on the command line. File permissions on the generated credential key are best-effort on Windows because the owner-only mode the code requests has no exact equivalent. Everything else, including the embedded database, the plugin downloads and the port override argument, works the same way.

Diagnosing a server that will not start. The most common failure is that port 8080 is already in use, which surfaces as a bind exception during startup and an immediate exit. Find the process holding the port and stop it, or start this server on another port with --server.port. A second failure mode is an incompatible Java runtime: anything older than 17 fails to load the compiled classes and reports an unsupported class file version. Check the active runtime with java -version, remembering that a shell may resolve a different runtime than an IDE does. A third cause is a working directory the process cannot write to, which prevents the SQLite database from being created and produces a datasource error on boot. If the application starts but search returns a not-ready response, the problem is not deployment at all: the embedding model or the vector store plugin has not been installed yet, and the Plugins page will say so. Schema warnings mentioning a duplicate column are expected on an existing database and are safe to ignore.

Upgrading an existing installation. Stop the running server, replace target/mcp-server.jar with the new archive and start it again with java -jar target/mcp-server.jar. The database is upgraded in place on boot: the schema script runs every start and is written so that re-running it is harmless, adding any new tables and columns while tolerating the ones that already exist. That tolerance is why the startup log prints warnings about duplicate columns on an upgraded database; they indicate the migration worked, not that it failed. Take a copy of data/mcpserver.db before upgrading if the workspace matters, because there is no downgrade path once new columns exist. Downloaded plugin assets such as the embedding model and the native vector extension survive an upgrade and are not re-fetched. Connector credentials also survive, since they are encrypted with a key stored beside the database rather than inside the archive. Configuration overrides supplied as launch arguments must be repeated when the new version is started; they are not persisted anywhere.

Connecting a Confluence Cloud site. Create a connection of type Confluence and give it the base URL of the site, which for Cloud ends in .atlassian.net. Authentication uses the account email address as the username together with an API token generated from Atlassian account settings; a password will not work against Cloud. The deployment type is detected automatically when the connection is tested, so there is nothing to select by hand. Once the test succeeds the connection moves to a connected state and an initial backfill crawls existing pages and ingests them as ACL-tagged chunks. Change detection on Cloud relies on delta polling: the scheduler re-queries content modified since the stored cursor on a fixed interval. Webhook registration is not available on Cloud because subscribing to events there requires publishing a Connect or Forge app, which this server deliberately does not do. The practical consequence is that a Cloud connection notices edits within one polling interval rather than immediately, and cannot reliably observe deletions at all, because the content search API returns no tombstone for a page that has been removed.

Connecting a Confluence Server or Data Center instance. Create a connection of type Confluence and give it the base URL of the instance, typically a self-hosted host name rather than an atlassian.net address. Authentication uses the ordinary account username and password; API tokens are a Cloud concept and are not used here. The deployment type is detected automatically when the connection is tested. Once the test succeeds an initial backfill crawls existing pages and ingests them as ACL-tagged chunks, exactly as on Cloud. Change detection differs in one important way: Server and Data Center support webhook registration, so the server can subscribe to page created, updated and removed events and react within seconds instead of waiting for the next poll. Webhooks require a publicly reachable callback URL, configured through the connector webhook base URL setting; when that setting is blank the connection falls back to delta polling. The removed event is the only reliable way to purge a deleted page's chunks, which is why a Server connection keeps the index cleaner over time than a Cloud one.

Connecting a Jira Cloud site. Create a connection of type Jira and give it the base URL of the site, which for Cloud ends in .atlassian.net. Authentication uses the account email address as the username together with an API token generated from Atlassian account settings; a password will not work against Cloud. Deployment type is detected automatically on test. Issue search on current Jira Cloud goes through the cursor-paginated JQL search endpoint, because Atlassian retired the classic search endpoint on Cloud during 2025; the connector probes the modern endpoint first and caches the answer per connection so only the first call pays for a failed probe. Backfill walks every issue matching the connection's scope and ingests summary, description and comment fields as chunks tagged with the project key. Change detection uses JQL delta polling against the stored cursor. Webhook registration is unavailable on Cloud for the same reason as Confluence: it would require a published Connect or Forge app. Edits therefore appear within one polling interval, and an issue edited in place replaces its existing chunks rather than duplicating them.

Connecting a Jira Server or Data Center instance. Create a connection of type Jira and give it the base URL of the instance, typically a self-hosted host name rather than an atlassian.net address. Authentication uses the ordinary account username and password; API tokens are a Cloud concept and are not used here. Deployment type is detected automatically on test. Issue search on Server and Data Center uses the classic offset-paginated search endpoint, which remains supported there even though Cloud has retired it; the connector falls back to this path automatically when the modern cursor-paginated endpoint is not available. Backfill walks every issue matching the connection's scope and ingests summary, description and comment fields as chunks tagged with the project key. Change detection can use webhooks: Server and Data Center allow the server to register for issue created, updated and deleted events, so changes are picked up in seconds. The deleted event purges the issue's chunks, which delta polling alone cannot do. Webhooks need a publicly reachable callback URL; without one the connection falls back to polling.

Diagnosing a connection that will not sync. Start with the connection's status and last error, which the Connections page shows directly. An authentication failure on an atlassian.net host almost always means a password was supplied where an API token is required, or the username field holds an account name rather than the account email address. An authentication failure against a self-hosted host usually means the opposite mistake. A connection that tests successfully but ingests nothing normally has a scope that matches no content, or points at a space or project the account cannot read. If edits are not appearing, check whether the connection is disabled: a disabled connection is simply excluded from the polling query, which is the entire pause mechanism, and it produces no error of its own. Deletions that never propagate are expected on Cloud, where no webhook is available and the content search API emits no tombstones. Certificate errors against an internal host mean the issuing authority is not trusted by the runtime; supply the certificate through the TLS configuration rather than disabling verification.

Uploading a document so it becomes searchable. Drag a file into a folder on the Files page, or use the upload control in that folder. The upload is stored, then handed to the ingestion pipeline, which is the single entry point every content source shares. The pipeline extracts text, splits it into chunks, computes an embedding for each chunk and writes the chunk together with its lexical and vector index entries in one operation. Progress is visible while ingestion runs, and the document becomes searchable as soon as its chunks are written, typically within seconds for a small file and a minute or two for a large one. Every chunk records the folder's visibility as ACL tags at the moment it is written, so permission metadata is never backfilled later. Re-uploading a changed file replaces that file's chunks in place rather than adding a second copy, because replacement is keyed on the source file identifier. Deleting the file purges its chunks, so stale content does not linger in results.

How documents are split into chunks. Splitting is structure aware rather than a blind fixed-size cut: headings, speaker turns and ticket fields are treated as natural boundaries so a chunk tends to contain one coherent idea. The target size is roughly 450 tokens with an 80-token overlap between neighbours, and the overlap exists so that a sentence spanning a boundary is still fully present in at least one chunk. The target is deliberately below the embedding model's 512-token window, because a chunk larger than that window is silently truncated before the embedding is computed and the tail of it becomes unsearchable by meaning. Very short documents produce a single chunk. Very long ones produce many, each carrying the same source name, path and permission metadata so a result can always be traced back to its origin. Chunk position is recorded, which is what lets the interface group several matching chunks under the one document they came from instead of presenting them as unrelated results.

Which file formats can be ingested. Plain text formats are handled directly, including txt, markdown, csv, json, xml, yaml and html, with html tags stripped before the text is split. Binary office formats go through a document parsing library that covers PDF, Word in both docx and legacy doc form, Excel, PowerPoint, rich text and OpenOffice documents. Extraction quality depends on the source: a text-based PDF extracts cleanly, whereas a scanned PDF that contains only page images yields nothing, because no optical character recognition is performed. Spreadsheets extract as cell text without formulas or formatting, which is usually enough to answer a question about a value but not about how it was calculated. Archives are expanded and their supported members ingested individually. A file whose type cannot be recognised is stored but not indexed, so it remains downloadable from the Files page while never appearing in search results.

Retention for a standard workspace. Content ingested into a standard workspace is retained for 30 days after its source is deleted, after which the chunks are purged permanently and cannot be recovered from within the application. The 30-day window exists so that an accidental deletion can be undone by an administrator without restoring a database backup. Retention is measured from the deletion event, not from the ingestion date, so a document that lived in the workspace for a year still gets the full 30 days once removed. The policy applies uniformly to uploaded files and to content pulled from connected systems. Search never returns content that is inside its retention window but already deleted; the window governs how long the rows survive for recovery, not how long they stay findable. Changing the retention period affects future deletions only and does not resurrect content whose window has already elapsed.

Retention for an extended workspace. Content ingested into an extended workspace is retained for 90 days after its source is deleted, after which the chunks are purged permanently and cannot be recovered from within the application. The 90-day window suits teams with a compliance obligation to keep material available for a full quarter after removal. Retention is measured from the deletion event, not from the ingestion date, so a document that lived in the workspace for a year still gets the full 90 days once removed. The policy applies uniformly to uploaded files and to content pulled from connected systems. Search never returns content that is inside its retention window but already deleted; the window governs how long the rows survive for recovery, not how long they stay findable. Changing the retention period affects future deletions only and does not resurrect content whose window has already elapsed.

How hybrid retrieval works. A query runs down two independent legs at once. The vector leg embeds the query with the same model used at ingestion time and finds the nearest chunks by cosine similarity, which is what makes a question phrased in one vocabulary match a document written in another. The lexical leg runs a full-text search over the same chunks and finds exact term matches, which is what makes an identifier, an acronym or a product name land on the right document. Each leg returns its own ranked list of about forty candidates. The two lists are merged by reciprocal rank fusion, which scores an item by the reciprocal of its position in each list rather than by the raw scores, because a cosine distance and a text-relevance score are not on comparable scales. An item ranked highly by both legs therefore rises above an item that only one leg found. The merged candidates then go to the reranker for final ordering.

Exact matching and the lexical leg. The lexical leg exists because embeddings are poor at exactly the queries people expect a search box to nail: a ticket key, an error code, an acronym, a file name, a configuration key. Those tokens carry little semantic content, so the vector leg often ranks them no better than chance, while a term index matches them precisely. Common English words are stripped before matching, and terms of two characters or fewer are ignored, so a query made entirely of stop words falls back to the vector leg alone. Matching is stemmed, meaning a search for deploying also matches deployed and deployment. The lexical leg keeps working when the embedding model or the vector store is unavailable, which is why the application still answers keyword searches while running in a degraded state — the response says so explicitly rather than silently returning worse results.

Reranking and final ordering. The candidates surviving fusion are re-scored by a cross-encoder, which reads the query and a candidate chunk together rather than comparing two independently computed vectors. That joint reading is markedly more accurate than the retrieval score and is why the final ordering can differ substantially from the merged one. Because the model is comparatively expensive it only sees a bounded candidate window rather than the whole corpus, which means a chunk neither retrieval leg surfaced can never be recovered by reranking. A small bonus is added when the query's terms appear in the document's file name, applied before the final sort so that a displayed score always agrees with the position it produced. Results scoring below a relevance floor are dropped entirely unless they contain a large share of the query's terms, which is what allows a question with no good answer to return nothing at all instead of a page of weak matches.

Augmenting search with live web results. The web toggle on the search page adds public web content to the evidence for a query. When it is on, the query is expanded into several intent-preserving variants and sent to a locally running meta-search process, candidate URLs are de-duplicated, a bounded set of pages is fetched over a request path guarded against server-side request forgery, the text is extracted and each page is scored for semantic relevance to the original question, along with authority, freshness, corroboration between sources and domain diversity. Web evidence is held in memory for the duration of the request and is never written to the chunk store, so it cannot pollute the workspace index or leak into an unrelated search. Local and web results are ranked on the same relevance scale and clearly labelled by origin. The toggle requires the meta-search plugin to be installed and running; without it the search proceeds using local knowledge only and says so.

Teaching search from feedback. Each search result carries a thumbs-up and thumbs-down control, and the application also notes lighter signals such as expanding a source group or following a source link. Those signals are recorded against the exact ranking that produced them, so a rating is always attributed to the positions the user actually saw. Repeated feedback on similar questions builds a preference: a result rated helpful for one question is nudged upward the next time a similar question is asked, and one rated unhelpful is nudged down. The nudge is bounded and applied after the relevance filter, so a negative rating can only lower a result's position and can never remove it from the results entirely — which means a rating given by mistake is always reversible. Preferences fade if they are not reinforced. Everything learned can be cleared from the Plugins page, and because the underlying ratings are kept separately it can also be rebuilt from them.

ACL tags on ingested chunks. An ACL tag is the permission metadata captured on every chunk at the moment it is written, derived from wherever the content came from: the folder's visibility for an upload, the connection and space for a Confluence page, the connection and project for a Jira issue. Tags are recorded on every intake path without exception and are never backfilled later, because reconstructing who could see a document at the time it was ingested is not possible after the fact. The tags travel with the chunk through retrieval and are returned alongside every result. Enforcement is a separate concern that activates with the authentication phase: until then the tag list is captured and carried but no filter is applied, and the server stays bound to the loopback address precisely because that filter is not yet in place. Capturing early and filtering later is a deliberate ordering — the reverse would leave existing content permanently untagged.

Permission labels on exported reports. A permission label is a classification string attached to a generated report or dashboard export, chosen by whoever creates the document, and it is unrelated to the ACL tags recorded during ingestion. Labels describe how a finished artefact may be circulated — internal, confidential, restricted — and are rendered into the exported file's header so the classification travels with the copy. They do not filter anything, they do not affect which content a query can retrieve, and applying a label to a report has no effect on the permissions of the underlying source documents. Because the two concepts are easy to confuse, remember the distinction by where each is set: an ACL tag is derived automatically from a source system at ingestion time, whereas a permission label is typed by a person at export time. Changing a label re-renders the export and nothing else.

Why the server binds to the loopback address. The application listens on 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces, and this is a deliberate guardrail rather than an oversight. There is no authentication layer yet: no login, no session, no token validation, and no per-user identity, so any request that reaches the port is fully trusted. Binding to loopback means that only processes on the same machine can reach it. Do not change the bind address, place the server behind a reverse proxy that exposes it publicly, or forward the port from another host, until the authentication phase lands and requests carry a verified identity. The same reasoning is why permission filtering is not yet applied to search results even though the metadata to apply it is already captured: with no authenticated user there is nobody to filter for. Treat the current posture as trusted single machine, not trusted internal network.

The audit log. Every tool invocation, approval, rejection, execution and failure is written to an audit record with a timestamp, the actor, the tool involved, the arguments supplied and a summary of the outcome or the error. The log is queryable by actor, by tool, by event type and by date range, and it is append-only in practice: nothing in the application updates or deletes an existing entry. The actor recorded is client-declared for now, taken from a request header and defaulting to a generic web user, because there is no authenticated identity to bind it to; entries become trustworthy as identity once the authentication phase supplies a verified subject. Failures are logged with the same weight as successes, so an audit trail shows attempted actions rather than only completed ones. The log is stored in the same embedded database as everything else and grows without an automatic retention policy.

How connection credentials are stored. A credential supplied when creating a connection — a password or an API token — is encrypted before it is written to the database using AES-256-GCM, an authenticated cipher, so a tampered ciphertext fails to decrypt rather than silently yielding wrong plaintext. The encryption key is generated on first use and written to a key file beside the database, with owner-only file permissions where the operating system supports them. This is a deliberate and documented scope limit: there is no integration with a secrets manager or a hardware-backed key store, which means anyone who can read both the database file and the key file can recover the credentials. That is an acceptable posture for a single trusted machine and would not be for a shared host. Credentials are never returned by the API, never written to logs and never rendered in the interface once saved; the interface shows only whether a credential is present.

Importing a Postman collection. Create a connection of the API collection type and supply a Postman v2.1 collection, either by uploading the exported file or by giving a URL that serves it. Each request in the collection becomes one callable tool, named from the application slug and the request slug so the resulting handle is stable and predictable. Folders in the collection become tool categories. A JSON schema is generated per request from its parameters, path variables, query string and body, and that schema is what validates arguments at call time. Read-only requests are enabled automatically on import because they cannot change anything. Requests that modify state arrive in a pending status and stay uncallable until an administrator approves them. Authentication blocks inside the collection are not imported: the administrator picks an auth mode on the connection and supplies the credential separately, so a token accidentally exported inside a collection file never becomes live configuration.

Importing an OpenAPI specification. Create a connection of the API collection type and supply an OpenAPI 3.x document as a file or a URL; a Swagger UI page URL is also accepted and resolved to the underlying specification through several strategies. Each operation becomes one callable tool, named from the application slug and the operation slug. Tags in the specification become tool categories. A JSON schema is generated per operation from its parameters and request body, and that schema validates arguments at call time. Local references inside the document are resolved with a depth limit to guard against cycles; a reference to an external document degrades to an untyped object rather than failing the import. GET operations are enabled automatically on import, while state-changing operations arrive pending and require approval. Security schemes declared in the specification are not imported as credentials: the administrator chooses an auth mode and supplies the secret on the connection.

Approving a state-changing tool. A tool that modifies a remote system never executes straight from a search box. Typing an invocation returns a preview showing the resolved target, the arguments that would be sent and the effect that would follow, together with a single-use confirmation token that expires. Execution happens only when the confirmation is submitted with that token, and the token cannot be replayed: a second attempt with the same token is rejected, which is what makes a duplicated click harmless. An idempotency key accompanies the execution so a retried request cannot create two of the same object. Every step — invocation, preview, approval or rejection, execution, outcome — is written to the audit log. A rejected or expired token produces no side effect at all. Read-only tools bypass this flow because there is nothing to confirm, which is why they can be enabled automatically on import while write tools cannot.

Grouping applications and endpoints. A group is a user-defined set that can contain whole applications, individual endpoints, or a mixture of both drawn from several applications. Groups exist to make a large imported surface navigable and to allow batch operations: enabling or disabling a group applies the change to every endpoint it contains, one at a time, so the usual per-tool rules still apply. A group has a slug that stays stable when the group is renamed, which means saved queries referencing it keep working after a rename. The slug is resolvable in the application position of the search grammar, so a group can be addressed the same way an application can. When a group slug collides with an application slug the application wins, so adding a group can never break an existing query. Groups hold membership only; deleting a group removes the grouping and leaves every application and endpoint untouched.

Authentication modes for imported APIs. A connection of the API collection type supports four modes. None sends no credential at all. Basic sends a username and password using HTTP basic authentication. Bearer sends a token in the authorization header with the bearer prefix. API key header sends a token in a header whose name the administrator specifies, which covers the many APIs that use a custom header instead of a standard scheme. The chosen credential is encrypted at rest with the same cipher used for connector credentials. An individual endpoint can override the connection's mode with its own, which covers an application whose endpoints authenticate differently; leaving the endpoint's mode unset means it inherits from the connection. OAuth2 flows are a reserved mode that is not implemented. Every outbound call is built from the connection's base URL plus the endpoint template, so an imported endpoint cannot be pointed at a different host.

The report query language. Queries are written as pipelines: a dataset is produced by a source stage and then transformed by a sequence of stages joined by a pipe operator, each of which takes a dataset and returns a dataset. Because every stage accepts every dataset there is no matrix of which verb may target which kind of input, which removes an entire category of error that a statement-per-verb grammar produces. The parser never throws on bad input. It returns a partial tree with error nodes in place of what it could not read, plus a list of diagnostics that each carry a stable code, a severity and a source span, and it resynchronises at statement and stage boundaries so a single typo cannot blank the rest of the analysis. That fault tolerance is what makes live editing viable: the editor keeps offering completions and error markers for the parts of a query that are still well formed while you are midway through typing another part.

Pipeline stages in the report query language. A query begins with a source stage that names a request or a collection, and continues through transformation stages. Filtering keeps rows matching a predicate. Selection chooses and renames columns. Expansion flattens a nested field into rows. Grouping aggregates with counts, sums and averages. Sorting and limiting shape the output. Joining combines two datasets on a key. Because the stage set is small and closed, the set of tokens that may legally follow a pipe is small and closed too, which is exactly the property that makes useful autocompletion possible after each stage boundary. The pipe operator doubles as an error recovery point, so a mistake inside one stage does not prevent the following stages from being understood. Stages are presentation free: the same query drives an interactive dashboard and a spreadsheet export without change.

The insight document format. An insight is a single document that mixes prose and queries. It opens with front matter declaring a title, a default connection and any typed parameters the document accepts, followed by markdown prose interleaved with fenced query blocks and component tags that render results as charts or tables. Values computed by a query can be interpolated into the prose, so a sentence can state a number that updates whenever the document runs. Raw HTML is rejected: only markdown and the known component tags are accepted, which removes a cross-site scripting surface and the sanitiser that would otherwise have to be maintained alongside it. A document is saved as its source text, so it is diffable and reviewable, and the most recent rendered result is stored alongside it so reopening the document shows the previous run rather than an empty panel while the queries re-execute.

Chart components in an insight. Charts are declared as component tags naming the dataset and the fields to plot. The available forms are deliberately limited and several constraints are structural rather than advisory: there is no second axis property, so a dual-axis chart cannot be expressed at all; colour is requested by role — categorical, sequential, diverging, status — rather than by hex value, so a document cannot hard-code a colour that breaks in a different theme; a filter element is invalid inside a chart, so a per-chart filter is unrepresentable; and every chart emits an accessible table alongside it which cannot be switched off. Categorical series beyond eight fold automatically into an other bucket. Scatter and bubble forms error rather than warn past three series. Charts are drawn as inline vector graphics with no external charting dependency.

Exporting an insight to a spreadsheet. A saved insight can be projected into an Excel workbook. Each dataset becomes a sheet, and charts are emitted as native spreadsheet charts wherever the form allows it, falling back to the accessible table twin when it does not. A chart is never exported as a rasterised image, because producing one would require a headless browser and this application deliberately runs as a single process with no such dependency. Prose sections become annotated header rows so the exported workbook remains readable on its own. The export is a projection of the document rather than its primary form: the interactive dashboard is what the query language is designed around, and the workbook is generated from the same presentation-free queries. Parameters declared in the front matter are resolved before export, so the workbook captures one specific parameterisation rather than a live document.

The model context protocol endpoint. The server exposes an MCP endpoint on the same process and the same port as the web interface, registered as a servlet at the /mcp path, so it inherits the loopback binding and needs no second server. The transport is streamable HTTP. A client connects by initialising, listing the available tools and calling one; the standard handshake works with any compliant client. The integration surface is deliberately two classes — a bootstrap and a bridge that listens for tool change events and updates the registration — so that if the protocol library breaks, only MCP exposure degrades while the REST API and in-application search keep working. Tool registration is live: enabling or disabling a tool updates the exposed list without a restart, and a call re-reads the tool at invocation time so a tool disabled between listing and calling cannot still execute.

What the MCP endpoint exposes. Two kinds of tool appear to a connected client. The first is the built-in knowledge search, which wraps the same retrieval pipeline the web interface uses and returns cited context — excerpt, source title, source URL, score and provenance — without any generated answer text, because the server never writes prose on behalf of a model. The second is every enabled imported endpoint, each carrying the JSON schema generated at import so a client can construct a valid call. State-changing endpoints only appear once approved, so an MCP client cannot reach a write tool that an administrator has not reviewed. Retrieved content is wrapped in explicit delimiters with a provenance label before it is returned, which isolates it as data and is the defence against instructions embedded in an ingested document being read as commands by the model consuming it.

The embedding model plugin. Semantic search needs a model that turns text into vectors, and this one runs in the server's own process rather than calling out to a hosted service, so no content leaves the machine to be indexed. The model is a long-context text embedding model producing 768-dimensional vectors with a 512-token input window, exported to a portable inference format and executed through an in-process runtime. It is downloaded on demand from the Plugins page rather than shipped inside the archive, because the weights are far larger than the application itself. Installation shows progress and the model becomes usable as soon as it finishes. Until then search still answers, using the keyword index alone, and says explicitly that semantic matching is off rather than silently returning weaker results. The model choice sits behind a swappable interface, so a different provider can be substituted without touching the retrieval code.

The vector store plugin. Vector similarity search is provided by a native extension loaded into the embedded SQLite database, which keeps the entire storage layer in one file with no separate database server to install or operate. The extension is a small native library downloaded on demand from the Plugins page and loaded at runtime, at which point a virtual table for vectors is created alongside the ordinary chunk table and the keyword index. Because loadable extensions are scoped to the connection that loaded them, the application deliberately uses a single shared database connection rather than a pool; a fresh connection per request would not see the vector table at all. Until the extension is installed the vector leg of retrieval is unavailable and search runs on the keyword index alone. Uninstalling does not delete stored embeddings, so reinstalling restores semantic search without re-ingesting anything.

The web search plugin. Live web augmentation needs a search backend, and this one is a locally installed open-source meta-search process rather than a commercial search API, so queries are not sent to a third-party account tied to this workspace. The plugin manages that process for you: installing it fetches and configures the software, and starting it launches a child process on a loopback port. Readiness is determined by an actual health request rather than by whether the process was launched, so a process that started but is not answering is reported as not ready. A process identifier is recorded so a running instance can be adopted after the application restarts instead of being orphaned or duplicated. The plugin is optional: with it stopped or uninstalled the web toggle on the search page reports that augmentation is unavailable and searches proceed against local knowledge only.
